articleBody:
Miami's restaurant landscape tells a story written in rice, black beans, and slow-roasted pork. According to Eater Miami, Cuban food isn't simply one cuisine among many in the city—it is inseparable from what Miami is. The publication's guide to the city's best Cuban restaurants underscores how waves of Cuban immigrants, especially from the 1960s forward, have fundamentally shaped not just the food available on local tables, but the rhythm and character of the city itself.

Little Havana, the neighborhood named after Cuba's capital and largest city, stands as the geographical and cultural heart of this culinary legacy. Home to many Cuban exiles and immigrants from Central and South America, Little Havana emerged as a vital community hub where families transplanted their cooking traditions, recipes passed down through generations, and the flavors of home. What began as immigrant communities preserving their heritage through food has evolved into a destination that defines Miami's identity for both residents and visitors.

The restaurants that populate Eater Miami's roundup represent more than business ventures—they are repositories of cultural memory and sites where daily life continues uninterrupted from one generation to the next. These establishments serve the breakfast cafecito and Cuban sandwich that punctuate morning routines, host family celebrations, and maintain connections to an island and a way of life that shaped everyone who walks through their doors.

Cuban cuisine in Miami has developed its own distinctive character, informed by local ingredients, the restaurant industry's evolution, and the creative innovations of chefs who grew up eating their families' cooking and later professionalized those traditions. The food scene has become self-sustaining, passed between generations and continually reinforced by immigration patterns and community pride.

For Miami residents, Cuban restaurants function as more than dining options—they are gathering places where culture, memory, and sustenance intersect. For the broader city, they represent a living archive of immigration, adaptation, and the ways that communities build home in new places through the rituals and flavors they carry with them.

Miami's bar scene is embracing a new chapter as vermouth and sherry-based cocktails move into the spotlight alongside the rum and agave spirits that have long defined the city's drinking culture. According to Eater Miami, recent bar openings are introducing classic Spanish cocktails and sophisticated fortified wine drinks to a market hungry for refined alternatives to the tropical concoctions that made Miami famous.

As a gateway between the U.S., the Caribbean, and Latin America, Miami has built its reputation on diverse flavors—rum and agave spirits mingling with notes of citrus and exotic fruits. That foundation remains strong, but bartenders across the city are now layering in European traditions. Vermouth, an aromatized fortified wine flavored with botanicals and produced mainly in Italy, France, and Spain, has emerged as a key player in this evolution. The modern versions of vermouth were first produced in the mid- to late 18th century in Turin, Italy, and their arrival in Miami's bars marks a deliberate nod to classical cocktail craft.

The shift reflects both changing consumer tastes and the maturation of Miami's hospitality scene. Bartenders are no longer content to rest on tropical recipes; they're exploring the depth and complexity that sherry and vermouth bring to the cocktail canon. Spanish cocktails, in particular, bridge the gap between Miami's Latin American heritage and European sophistication, creating a natural fit for a city defined by cultural crossroads.

With the third-largest skyline in the U.S. and a metropolitan area of roughly 6.39 million residents, Miami has always attracted ambitious hospitality concepts. These new bars represent the latest wave of that ambition, suggesting that the city's drinking culture will continue to deepen and diversify in the years ahead.

articleBody:
Miami's premier dining promotion is back. The Greater Miami Convention & Visitors Bureau has announced that Miami Spice Restaurant Month—the region's flagship culinary event—will run for two months this year, from August 1 through September 30, 2026. The 25th edition marks a significant expansion of the program, which now includes more than 300 participating restaurants and introduces a new reserve tier to the traditional offerings.

Miami Spice has long been a fixture on the local calendar, drawing both residents and visiting tourists eager to experience the city's diverse dining landscape at reduced prices. The core concept remains straightforward: participating restaurants offer three-course prix-fixe menus at a minimum of 30% savings off regular pricing. This year's expansion reflects the program's continued growth and the increasing appetite for curated dining experiences that deliver value without sacrificing quality.

The introduction of a reserve tier represents the most notable structural change to the program in recent memory. While the GMCVB has not detailed the specific mechanics of the reserve category, the addition signals an effort to tier the participating restaurants by level of prestige or demand, potentially allowing diners to book experiences at some of Miami's most sought-after establishments during the promotion period. Such a move could help balance interest across the full roster of participating venues and ensure that both casual eateries and high-end establishments benefit from the program's promotional power.

According to Miami Curated, the expansion to over 300 restaurants represents a substantial increase in participation compared to previous years, underscoring the program's appeal to the local dining community. The extended two-month window—longer than some previous iterations—also provides restaurants with additional time to capture diners' attention and allows consumers more flexibility in planning their culinary calendar.

The timing of Miami Spice in the late summer and early fall positions it strategically as the region transitions from its slower summer season into the busier fall and holiday periods. For restaurants, the program serves as an engine to drive covers during a traditionally quieter window. For diners, it offers an accessible entry point to sample restaurants they might not otherwise visit or to revisit established favorites at a discount.

whatHappening: Miami Curated has published a guide to five elegant bars in Miami, drawing inspiration from luxury bar culture and timeless design. whoInvolved: Miami Curated is the publication behind this guide. The St. Regis New York, a luxury hotel developed by John Jacob Astor IV and completed in 1904, serves as the reference point—it is a Forbes five-star and AAA five-diamond rated property operated by Marriott International.

articleBody:
Miami's bar scene is drawing comparison to some of the nation's most storied cocktail lounges, according to Miami Curated, which recently highlighted five exceptional bars in the city that embody elegance and refined hospitality. The publication used the King Cole Bar at Manhattan's St. Regis as a touchstone—a venue where stepping inside feels like entering a different era, one in which elegance was not merely fashionable but a fundamental way of life.

The St. Regis New York, located at 2 East 55th Street in Midtown Manhattan, has long represented the gold standard of luxury hospitality since its completion in 1904. Designed by the architecture firm Trowbridge & Livingston for developer John Jacob Astor IV, the hotel was expanded in 1927 with an annex to the east designed by Sloan & Robertson. Today, operated by Marriott International, the St. Regis maintains its five-star Forbes and five-diamond AAA ratings, underscoring its sustained position as a premier destination for discerning travelers and guests seeking sophisticated experiences.

The King Cole Bar, housed within the St. Regis, exemplifies a design philosophy centered on immersion in historical glamour. Its enduring appeal lies in its refusal to abandon elegance in favor of contemporary casualness—a choice that has become increasingly deliberate as fashion and design have shifted toward informality and minimalism across the broader culture.

Miami Curated's selection of five Miami bars suggests that this appetite for refined, elegant spaces extends beyond New York. The guide appears to celebrate establishments that prioritize atmosphere, craftsmanship, and a sense of occasion—qualities that harken back to mid-century cocktail culture and the notion that entering a bar should feel like a retreat into sophistication rather than a casual drop-in.

For Miami's hospitality landscape, this curation underscores a market for venues that resist the tide of casual design. Even as contemporary culture embraces laid-back aesthetics, there remains a clientele willing to seek out and patronize spaces that demand and reward a certain standard of presentation and comportment. The comparison to King Cole Bar, with its historical pedigree and timeless appeal, sets a high bar—both literally and figuratively—for what Miami establishments are offering to their guests.
